p.src: Lecture 113 asked what keeps people once they join. Lecture 116 adds the next operating question: once the team exists, what lets it actually work together when people are not in the same room? The interview is introduced as a question about the next five to ten years in technology, but the answer develops one tighter claim. Part of the future is already here, the pandemic accelerated it, remote work is the visible change, and collaboration is the deeper category.

p.src:
Let $B=\text{effective internet speed or bandwidth},
\qquad
C=\text{capability of collaboration tools},$ $P_{\mathrm{comm}}=\text{practical productivity of the communication layer},
\qquad
V_{\mathrm{remote}}=\text{viability of remote work}.$ A cautious reconstruction of the lecture’s mechanism is $\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{comm}} &= g(B,C),\\
\frac{\partial g}{\partial B} &> 0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial g}{\partial C} > 0.\end{aligned}$ The transcript gives no numerical calibration and no measured threshold. The point is only monotone: faster connectivity and better tools increase the practical productivity of communication.

p.src: Why is remote work viable now when it was not viable before?

u.src: Why is remote work viable now when it was not viable before?
en: Why is remote work viable now when it was not viable before?

p.src: Because the enabling layer improved. The speaker names fast internet access speeds and collaborative tools, then grounds the claim in ordinary products: Zoom, Slack, and even email. The point is not that one app changed the world by itself. The point is that the communication stack became productive enough to support real coordination across distance.

p.src: This section should stay distinct from the book’s media-leverage thread. There, technology expands reach outward: audience, recruiting, deal flow, or brand visibility. Here, technology keeps the inside of the company coherent. The founder’s question is therefore not only, How do we get attention? It is also, How does work remain joined together when distance intervenes?

p.src:
In the lecture’s own order, the final judgment is clear: $\text{collaboration first},
\qquad
\text{remote work second}.$ That is the durable addition to the book. A distributed company is not defined mainly by where people sit. It is defined by whether communication has become strong enough for coordinated work to survive separation.
